0.title: That You May Know: The Epistle of Assurance
0.overview:
There is a letter in the New Testament that reads like the heartbeat of an old man who has seen everything and lost nothing. John — the apostle whom Jesus loved, the one who leaned against the Lord at the Last Supper, the one who stood at the foot of the cross when the others had fled (John 13:23; 19:26) — writes at the end of a long life with the urgency of a man who knows that what he carries is the most important thing in the world. He has handled the Word of Life with his own hands. He has seen the glory. And he cannot be silent.

The First Epistle of John was written to a community under assault — not from Rome, but from within. Teachers had arisen who denied the full humanity of Christ, claiming that the eternal Son had not truly come in the flesh, that the spiritual and the material could not really meet. They were sophisticated, confident, and wrong. When they left the fellowship, John writes to those who remain, not to condemn the departed but to assure the faithful: you are not the ones who have missed it. The letter is saturated with the word "know" — used over thirty times. John wants his readers to know that they have eternal life, that they are in fellowship with the Father and the Son, that the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

But assurance in John is never cheap. It is tested by three great evidences that run through the letter like interwoven cords: the moral test (do you walk in the light, keeping his commandments?), the social test (do you love your brothers and sisters?), and the doctrinal test (do you confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh?). These are not conditions for salvation but symptoms of it — the fingerprints of new birth on a redeemed life. The person who has truly been born of God will love, will obey, and will confess. Not perfectly — John is the one who tells us that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves — but genuinely and persistently.

At the theological centre of the letter stands the cross. "The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin" (1:7). "He is the propitiation for our sins" (2:2). "He laid down his life for us" (3:16). "God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (4:10). John circles back to the atoning death of Christ again and again, because the cross is the ground of everything — fellowship, forgiveness, assurance, love. The love of God is not an abstraction in 1 John; it is a specific act: the sending of the Son into the world to bear the wrath that our sins deserved so that we might live through him.

1 John was written to produce settled, humble, joyful assurance in the hearts of those who have truly come to Christ — and such assurance, far from producing complacency, is the very fire that fuels a life of love.

1.title: The Word of Life and the God of Light
1.text: <sup>1</sup>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—<sup>2</sup>the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—<sup>3</sup>that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.<sup>4</sup>And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.<sup>5</sup>This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.<sup>6</sup>If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.<sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.<sup>8</sup>If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.<sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.<sup>10</sup>If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1.overview:
The letter opens with a declaration, not a greeting. John insists four times on the physical reality of what he witnessed: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. The eternal Word became someone John could hold. Against teachers who claimed a higher spiritual knowledge and despised the body, John’s answer is the incarnation.

The purpose is fellowship with the Father, the Son and one another. Then comes the first test: God is light, with no darkness at all. Any claim to know him that is comfortable with sin is self-deception. But the answer to sin is not despair. The blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin, and God forgives all who confess.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any command or warning, John rests the whole letter on one fact: the eternal Word became audible, visible and touchable. John is writing as a man who was there, who ate with him and touched him after he rose. And the purpose of his witness is not just correct information, but that his readers would share the fellowship he has with the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Incarnation as the Ground of Fellowship

The eternal life was heard, seen and touched. A Christ who did not truly come in the flesh could not truly atone, and fellowship with God rests on that fact.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Teachers were spiritualising Christ out of his humanity.

Now: The gospel is not a philosophy but a report of what was heard and seen.

verseByVerse.quote: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—
verseByVerse.commentary:
John announces the eternal Word of life, who existed from the beginning with the Father and then appeared in history, so that the apostles heard him, saw him and touched him. They testify to what they experienced.

Four senses. John piles up the evidence: heard, seen with our eyes, looked upon, touched with our hands. “Touched” is the most physical word he could use. The eternal life “was made manifest”: the pre-existent Son entered time and became visible.

Why it matters. The false teachers said the divine Christ only seemed to have a body. John answers with eyewitness testimony. A Christ who did not truly take flesh could not truly die for us. Christianity is not a philosophy or a feeling, but a report of what happened.
verseByVerse.note: The letter does not name its author, but its language is so close to John’s Gospel that it has long been received as the apostle John’s, written late in the first century, probably from Ephesus. Some had left the church denying that Jesus the Christ truly came in the flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John proclaims what he saw and heard so that his readers may share fellowship with the apostles, a fellowship that is with the Father and his Son Jesus Christ.

Fellowship. The word (koinōnia) means sharing a common life. The church is not a club that happens to worship God. Its deepest reality is communion with the Father and the Son, and so with one another. The gospel draws us into a circle of love that has existed from eternity.

On a Tuesday. You may feel that your church is just a group of very different people with little in common. John says what you share is far deeper than personality or background: you share the Father and the Son. That changes how you greet the person you find hardest to like.

verseByVerse.quote: And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes so that joy may be complete.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “your joy”; the ESV follows the better-attested “our joy”. The meaning is similar either way: the apostle’s joy is bound up with his readers’ sharing in the fellowship of vv. 1–3.

Joy as the goal. The letter will correct and warn, but its aim is joy, the joy Jesus prayed his people would have (John 17:13). Truth about God is meant to lead to gladness in God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — God Is Light: Walking in the Truth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first thing John says about God is not a comfort but a blinding claim: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” Then he exposes three things people say to live comfortably without facing that light: that they have fellowship with God while walking in darkness, that they have no sin, and that they have not sinned. But the light that exposes also heals. The blood of Jesus cleanses, and God forgives those who confess.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Light

Three claims keep people from the light: fellowship while walking in darkness, having no sin, never having sinned. The remedy is confession to a God who is faithful and just to forgive.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers claimed an enlightenment that placed them above sin.

Now: Honest confession, not self-defence, keeps a believer in fellowship with God.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message Christ gave the apostles is that God is pure light, with no darkness in him at all.

God is light. Light in Scripture means moral purity, truth and life (Psalm 27:1; 36:9). John does not say God is mostly light, or light in the ways that count. The double negative rules out any shadow of compromise in him. This is the ground of everything the letter teaches about sin, love and fellowship.

From him. John did not invent this. He heard it from Christ, the light of the world (John 8:12), whose life made it visible.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Claiming fellowship with God while living in darkness is a lie.

Walk. John means the direction of a life, not an occasional stumble. To claim closeness to the God of light while your life heads steadily into darkness is not a small inconsistency; it is untrue.

Doing the truth. In John, truth is not only believed but practised. A faith that never changes how you live has not understood the God it claims to know.

verseByVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we live openly in God’s light, we share fellowship with one another, and Jesus’ blood keeps cleansing us from every sin.

What walking in the light does not mean. It is not sinless perfection, since the same verse says we still need cleansing. It means living honestly before God, with no part of life sealed off from him.

Keeps cleansing. The verb is present tense: Christ’s blood goes on cleansing. Even those who walk in the light remain sinners who need his atonement every day, and it never runs out.

On a Tuesday. You snap at a colleague, then remember it on the drive home. Walking in the light means not explaining it away. Name it to God, thank him that Christ’s blood covers it, and apologise in the morning.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who claims to be without sin is deceiving himself, and the truth is not in him.

No sin now. Verse 8 denies present, ongoing sinfulness; verse 10 denies ever having sinned. The false teachers likely thought their enlightenment had lifted them above sin. John calls it self-deception: the lie starts within.

Is perfection possible in this life? Some in the Wesleyan tradition teach that a believer can reach “entire sanctification” and no longer sin knowingly. But John says we, including himself, and the next verse assumes Christians will need to confess. When he later says that “no one born of God makes a practice of sinning” (1 John 3:9), he means the settled direction of a life. The believer still sins, but no longer lives in it at peace.

verseByVerse.quote: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we confess our sins, God, who is faithful and just, will forgive them and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

Faithful and just. We might expect “merciful”. John says God is faithful: he promised forgiveness and keeps his word. And he is just: the penalty has been paid at the cross, so forgiving the one who confesses does not set justice aside but honours it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every sin must be named before it is forgiven, or that a believer who dies with an unconfessed sin is lost. Our standing was settled when we believed: Christ’s blood “cleanses us from all sin” (v. 7), and “there is therefore now no condemnation” (Romans 8:1). Confession is how a child keeps short accounts with his Father and enjoys his fellowship, not a ledger of unpaid debts.

On a Tuesday. A man has been carrying guilt for months over a lie he told his wife. He finally confesses it to God, and then to her. That evening he reads this verse and believes it. The weight has not been excused; it has been carried by Christ. Worship rises from that kind of relief.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Claiming never to have sinned makes God a liar, because his word says all have sinned.

The most extreme claim. This denies any history of sin at all. God has testified that “all have sinned” (Romans 3:23). To deny it is not a different opinion; it contradicts God.

Why the bad news matters. The person who sees no sin has no use for v. 9. The good news has not reached him because the bad news has not yet landed. Only those who know they are sick run to the Physician.

1.theology:
The Incarnation as Foundation. Everything in 1 John rests on the physical, historical, tangible reality of the incarnation. John's stacked verbs in verses 1–2 — heard, seen, looked upon, touched — are a theological rampart against every form of docetism (the heresy that Christ only appeared to be human). If Christ did not truly come in flesh, the blood shed on Calvary has no atoning value, the resurrection is a spirit's trick, and there is no real fellowship between God and humanity. The incarnation is not incidental to Christianity; it is its structural foundation. God became graspable so that we could grasp him — and through him, life.

The God Who is Light. John's declaration that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" has massive ethical implications. Fellowship with a God of absolute moral purity cannot coexist with a comfortable relationship with sin. The light of God is not a comfortable mood but a searching, penetrating, all-revealing reality. It is also a liberating one: in the light, where our sin is exposed, the blood of Jesus cleanses. Reformed theology has always insisted on the holiness of God as the backdrop against which the grace of God becomes luminous. You cannot appreciate the gospel without first standing in the light of who God is.
1.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had just experienced a painful split. People they had worshipped with, broken bread with, called brothers and sisters, had walked out. The departure of the false teachers left wounds and questions. Were the ones who stayed the ones who had missed the deeper truth? John's answer in chapter 1 is the apostolic testimony: we were there. We heard him, saw him, touched him. This is not speculation; it is witness. The assurance of the community rests not on their spiritual experiences but on the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses of the Word of Life.

Now: We live in a culture that treats the interior life as the truest life — feelings, impressions, spiritual experiences. The incarnation is John's counter-word: Christianity is tethered to history, to flesh, to blood, to an empty tomb. Our fellowship with God is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the historical reality of the Son of God made flesh. And the practice of confession — agreeing with God about what we are — is the daily discipline that keeps that fellowship living and real. Every day we come back to the same place: not to earn forgiveness, but to receive what has already been purchased.

2.title: Our Advocate, Our Obedience, Our Love
2.text: <sup>1</sup>My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.<sup>2</sup>He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.<sup>3</sup>And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.<sup>4</sup>Whoever says “I know him” but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him,<sup>5</sup>but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:<sup>6</sup>whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.<sup>8</sup>At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.<sup>9</sup>Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.<sup>10</sup>Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.<sup>11</sup>But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.<sup>12</sup>I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.<sup>13</sup>I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.<sup>14</sup>I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.<sup>15</sup>Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.<sup>16</sup>For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.<sup>17</sup>And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.<sup>18</sup>Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.<sup>19</sup>They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.<sup>20</sup>But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.<sup>21</sup>I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.<sup>22</sup>Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.<sup>23</sup>No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.<sup>24</sup>Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.<sup>25</sup>And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.<sup>26</sup>I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.<sup>27</sup>But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.<sup>28</sup>And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.<sup>29</sup>If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
2.overview: Chapter 2 moves in three steps. First, John wants his readers not to sin, but knows they will, and points them to their advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins. Second, he gives the first test of real faith: obedience. Not sinless perfection, but a life that keeps God’s commands and walks as Jesus walked, and that loves the brothers. Third, he warns against loving the world, which is passing away, and against the antichrists who have left the church, and he urges his readers to abide in what they heard from the beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Advocate and the Test of Knowing God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John aims at holiness: he writes so that his people will not sin. But he knows they will, so the provision comes with the command. We have an advocate with the Father, who pleads not our innocence but his own righteousness, and who is himself the propitiation that turned away God’s wrath. On that ground of grace, John gives the first test: those who know him keep his commandments and walk as he walked.
verseByVerse.theology:
Advocate and Propitiation

John writes so that believers will not sin, and provides for when they do: Jesus Christ the righteous pleads for us, and he is the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Separating the divine Christ from the suffering Jesus emptied the cross.

Now: Knowing God shows itself in keeping his commandments and walking as Jesus walked.

verseByVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes so that his dear children will not sin, but if they do, they have Jesus Christ, the righteous one, pleading their case before the Father.

Two truths held together. The aim is holiness; John will not lower the standard. But the provision for failure is already in place. The advocate is not an emergency measure but a permanent reality.

Advocate. The word (paraklētos) is the one Jesus used for the Holy Spirit (John 14:16). Here it is Christ himself, standing beside us before the Father. He is “the righteous”: he does not plead that we are innocent, but that he has paid.

What it does not mean. It does not mean sin is no longer serious. The advocate is for those who are fighting sin and failing, not a licence for those who have stopped fighting.
verseByVerse.note: “Advocate” is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit (“Helper”) in John’s Gospel; here it is Jesus himself pleading for us.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath against our sins, and not only ours but the sins of the whole world.

Propitiation. The word (hilasmos) means more than covering sin (expiation). It means turning away God’s holy anger against sin. That anger has not been overlooked; it has been absorbed by Christ.

“The whole world”. Christians differ on what this means for the extent of the atonement. One view, particular or definite atonement, holds that Christ died to secure the salvation of his people, as Scripture often says: he will “save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21); he lays down his life “for the sheep” (John 10:11). On this view, “the whole world” means not only the Jewish believers John writes to, but God’s children scattered among all nations, the very language John uses in his Gospel (John 11:51–52). The other view holds that Christ died for every person, the benefit becoming theirs when they believe, pointing to texts such as “a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6).

Godly Reformed and evangelical teachers have held both. On balance the first view is more likely: it reads John by John, and keeps the cross a death that actually saves those for whom Christ died. But both agree on the things that matter most for daily life: Christ’s death is of infinite worth; the offer of the gospel is sincerely made to everyone; no one who comes to him is ever turned away; and no one is saved any other way.

On a Tuesday. John wrote this verse to steady Christians who had failed. If your own sin is what weighs on you today, this verse is for you. There is an advocate, and the case he pleads is his own blood. No sin of yours outruns it. Bow and give thanks.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath.

verseByVerse.quote: And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We can be sure we know God if we keep his commandments.

A test, not a ladder. John is not saying that obedience earns a relationship with God. He is saying that real knowledge of God shows itself in obedience, because the will is being shaped by the one we know.

What it does not mean. The test is not whether we ever fail (we do; 1:8), but whether obedience is the settled direction of our desire and effort.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever claims to know God but disobeys him is lying, but in whoever keeps his word, God’s love has truly reached its goal. This is how we know we are in him.

Perfected. God’s love does not declare us righteous and then leave us as we were. It works in us until it is expressed in a life shaped by his word.

Assurance. The last clause matters: “by this we may know that we are in him.” A life of growing obedience is not only moral evidence; it is one of the ways God assures us that we belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever claims to live in Christ should live as Christ lived.

The pattern. John points to the actual life of Jesus in the Gospels: his love, obedience, humility, prayer and willingness to suffer. This is not self-improvement by willpower, but what union with him produces. Branches that abide in the vine begin to bear the vine’s fruit (John 15:5).

On a Tuesday. Faced with an irritating neighbour, the question is not “what are my rights?” but “how did Jesus treat people who were difficult?” Walking as he walked starts in small moments like this.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — The Old-New Commandment: Love and Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The command to love is both old and new. Old, because it was there from the beginning (Leviticus 19:18). New, because Christ has given it a new measure, “as I have loved you” (John 13:34), and because the new age has begun: the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining. The test of whether we are in the light is concrete: do we love our brother?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Old-New Commandment

The command to love is old, and new in Christ, because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The split in the church showed where the darkness was.

Now: Nursed grudges blind; love keeps the path clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is not giving a new command, but the old one they have had from the beginning: the word they have heard.

Against novelty. The false teachers offered new, advanced knowledge. John keeps returning to what the church heard from the start. The answer to spiritual novelty is not more sophistication, but deeper roots in the apostolic gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet the command is also new, because it is fulfilled in Christ and now in believers, as the darkness passes away and the true light is already shining.

New in Christ. The cross is now the measure of love. The command is “true in him” because he lived it perfectly, and “true in you” because the Spirit now produces it in believers.

The new age. The darkness is passing; the light is already shining. To love is not to strain against reality, but to live in line with the age that has dawned in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who claims to be in the light but hates a fellow believer is still in darkness.

The concrete test. John will not let us separate love for God from love for his people. Hatred here is a settled attitude, not a moment of irritation. A spirituality that enjoys God while holding contempt for the believers he has put beside us is self-deception.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves his brother lives in the light, and there is nothing in him to make him stumble.

Clear sight. Love keeps our moral vision clear. Hatred distorts how we see people and situations, and makes us trip. Love walks steadily.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever hates his brother is in darkness, walks in it, and has lost his way, because the darkness has blinded him.

Blinded. Hatred does not just cloud our sight for a moment; it takes it away. The hater cannot see because of the darkness he has chosen.

On a Tuesday. A man has refused to speak to his brother for years over an inheritance. He tells himself he is in the right. John warns him that the grudge itself is blinding him. The way back into the light begins with a phone call, and with remembering how much he himself has been forgiven.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Assurance for Every Stage of Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the tests, John pauses to reassure. He addresses little children, fathers and young men, and tells each what is already theirs: forgiveness, knowledge of the eternal Christ, and victory over the evil one through the word abiding in them. Assurance comes before further commands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance for Every Stage

Before further commands, John tells children, fathers and young men what is already theirs: forgiveness, knowledge of God, and victory over the evil one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were being told they needed something more.

Now: The newest believer needs first to hear that his sins are forgiven for Christ’s name’s sake.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes to all his children because their sins have been forgiven for the sake of Christ’s name.

The first word. Before any command, John declares grace. The verb means forgiven and remaining forgiven. The ground is “his name”: who Christ is and what he has done, not how long we have been believers or how well we are doing.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes to mature believers, who know the eternal Christ; to younger believers, who have defeated the evil one; and to children, who know the Father.

Three stages. The fathers are marked by depth: long years have rooted them in Christ rather than made them casual. The young men are marked by victory: in Christ they have overcome the evil one. The children know the Father, the most basic and precious knowledge of all.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John repeats his words to fathers and young men: the young are strong because God’s word lives in them, and they have overcome the evil one.

Strength from the word. The order matters. The young men are strong because the word of God abides in them. Scripture is not just information about spiritual warfare; it is the sword itself (Ephesians 6:17).

On a Tuesday. A young believer facing temptation late at night has a verse ready, memorised that morning. It is not magic. It is the living word abiding in him, and through it Christ gives strength to stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — Do Not Love the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “Do not love the world.” John does not mean God’s creation, which God loves, or a call to withdraw from culture. He means the world system organised against God, with its own values and desires. He names its three roots: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life. And he gives the decisive reason: the world is passing away, but whoever does God’s will abides for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
Do Not Love the World

The desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life are not from the Father. The world is passing away; whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Wealth and religion were on public display in the cities of Asia.

Now: Receive created things as gifts, but enthrone none of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not love the world or what is in it, because love for the world and love for the Father cannot live in the same heart.

Which world? Not the created world God made and loves (John 3:16), but human life organised in rebellion against him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we cannot enjoy good things. Everything God made is good and may be received with thanks (1 Timothy 4:4). The issue is what sits on the throne of the heart. Created things may be enjoyed as gifts, but none may be loved as god.

verseByVerse.quote: For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything the world offers, the cravings of the body, the greed of the eyes and arrogant pride in what we have, comes from the world, not from the Father.

Three streams. The desires of the flesh treat appetite as master. The desires of the eyes are covetousness, wanting what we see. The pride of life is boasting in our possessions and achievements, as if we needed no God.

An old pattern. Eve saw that the fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desired to make one wise (Genesis 3:6). Christ was tempted in the same three ways and conquered (Matthew 4:1–11).

On a Tuesday. Scrolling through adverts and influencers, notice how often each of the three is being stirred: “You deserve this”, “Look at this”, “Be admired”. Name it, put the phone down, and thank God for what you already have in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world and its desires are passing away, but whoever does God’s will lives for ever.

Passing away. The world is already in the process of ending. To love it is to invest in a building that is collapsing.

Abides. The one who does God’s will “abides forever”. That is the only permanence there is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Antichrists, Apostasy, and the Anointing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Antichrists have appeared and left the church, denying the Father and the Son. John turns this crisis into confidence. Their departure revealed that they never truly belonged. And ordinary believers have what the false teachers claimed and lacked: the anointing of the Holy Spirit, who teaches them the truth and keeps them in it. The answer to deception is to abide in what was heard from the beginning, and so in the Son and the Father.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Anointing

Those who left showed that they were never of the church. Every believer has the anointing of the Spirit, who keeps him in the truth he heard from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers offered superior knowledge.

Now: Beware any teaching that says Scripture, the Spirit and the church are not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the last hour. Just as they heard that antichrist is coming, many antichrists have already appeared, and that confirms the time.

The last hour. The final era began with Christ’s first coming. The appearance of many antichrists is a sign of it.

Who is the antichrist? “Antichrist” appears only in John’s letters. The prefix means both “against” and “in place of”: an opponent and a counterfeit. The many antichrists are false teachers who deny the Son (v. 22), and the spirit of antichrist is at work in every age (4:3). Paul describes a final “man of lawlessness” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8). The most likely reading is that the antichrist spirit, active throughout history, will come to a final expression in one person at the end.

What it does not mean. It does not invite us to guess which public figure is the antichrist. John’s concern is practical: recognise and reject any teaching that denies who Jesus is.
verseByVerse.note: “Antichrist” appears in the Bible only in John’s letters.

verseByVerse.quote: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They left the church, but they never really belonged to it. If they had, they would have stayed. Their leaving showed that none of them were truly part of us.

Revealed, not caused. Their departure did not make them false; it showed what they had been.

Can true believers fall away? Arminian Christians hold that they can, pointing to warnings such as Hebrews 6:4–6. But John explains what happened plainly: “if they had been of us, they would have continued with us.” Those truly born of God are kept by him, and continuing is the evidence of it. The warnings in Scripture are one of the means God uses to keep his people, not proof that they will be lost.

On a Tuesday. When a friend leaves the faith, it can make you fear you will too. This verse is both sobering and comforting. Ask whether you truly trust Christ, and if you do, rest in the God who keeps those who are his. And keep praying for your friend: he may yet be brought to real faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and all of you know the truth.

The anointing. This is almost certainly the Holy Spirit, given to every believer. John says all of them have knowledge, not just a spiritual elite.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “you know all things”; the ESV follows the better-supported “you all have knowledge”. The point is not that believers know everything, but that every believer, not only the teachers, has the Spirit’s gift of knowing the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes not because they do not know the truth, but because they do, and because no lie comes from the truth.

Confirmation. This is a letter of assurance. They need reminding firmly enough to resist the lie.

No lie is of the truth. The false teaching is not a different angle on the same reality. It is incompatible with the truth, and knowing the truth helps them see that.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The liar is the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ. Such a person is antichrist, denying both the Father and the Son.

The lie. The false teachers likely taught that the divine Christ came on the man Jesus at his baptism and left before the cross. John answers that Jesus is the Christ: one person, who truly died. To deny the Son is to lose the Father, because there is no way to the Father except through the Son (John 14:6).

verseByVerse.quote: No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who denies the Son has the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father too.

Inseparable. The Son is not one of several routes to God, or a helpful idea that can be adjusted while the Father is kept. He is the only one through whom the Father is known and reached.

On a Tuesday. A colleague says, “I believe in God, but I don’t see why Jesus matters.” Gently, John’s answer is that God has shown himself in his Son. To know the Father, we must come to the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep the message you heard from the beginning in your hearts. If it remains in you, you will remain in the Son and the Father.

Word and relationship. Holding fast to the apostolic gospel is not just intellectual tidiness. It is how we hold fast to Christ himself. Abide in the truth, and you abide in the one who is the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God has promised us is eternal life.

Eternal life. Not just endless existence, but the life of the age to come, God’s own life shared with his people, already begun in those who believe (John 5:24). It is secured by the faithfulness of the one who promised, and it is found in the Son (1 John 5:11–12).

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes these things because of those who are trying to lead them astray.

Naming the threat. The false teachers are not just mistaken; they are trying to deceive. Naming them clearly is an act of pastoral love. The most dangerous deceptions are the ones no one names, because they come wrapped in spiritual language and sincerity.

verseByVerse.quote: But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit they received lives in them, so they do not need anyone to teach them a new message. The Spirit teaches them the truth, so they should remain in Christ.

What it does not mean. John does not mean the church needs no teachers. Christ gave teachers to his church (Ephesians 4:11), and John himself is teaching in this letter. He means they do not need the extra, elite knowledge the false teachers offered. Nor does it mean new private revelation. The Spirit helps believers recognise and receive the apostolic word they already have.

On a Tuesday. When a slick new teaching comes along, you do not have to be a scholar to sense that it does not fit the Jesus you know from Scripture. Trust that inner witness, test it by the word, and talk to a mature Christian. Then abide in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — Abide in Him: The Returning King and the Family Likeness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends looking to Christ’s return. Abide in him now, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink back in shame. Then John introduces a theme for chapter 3: if God is righteous, those born of him will practise righteousness. We live like God’s children because we are his children.
verseByVerse.theology:
Abide in him

Abide in Christ so as to have confidence at his coming. Those born of the righteous God practise righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Christ’s appearing was still ahead.

Now: Live now as someone who will meet him face to face.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep abiding in Christ, so that when he appears we may face him with confidence, not hide in shame.

His appearing. The whole Christian life faces towards Christ’s return. John includes himself: “we”. The confidence is not earned by perfection, but grows from real, persevering union with Christ. The shame is that of meeting someone whose words you have ignored.

On a Tuesday. Imagine Christ returning this afternoon. Would you run to meet him or want to hide what you are doing? Do not answer with dread, but turn to him now. The one who is coming is the advocate of chapter 2:1.

verseByVerse.quote: If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you know that God is righteous, you can be sure that everyone who practises righteousness has been born of him.

Family likeness. The new birth is not only a change of status but a change of nature. Children resemble their Father.

What it does not mean. Doing right does not earn new birth. New birth produces right living. This is John’s first mention of being born of God, and he develops it in 3:4–10.

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The paired terms of 2:1–2 give us the two aspects of Christ's saving work seen from different angles. As advocate, he represents us before the Father — our case is in his hands, and he is qualified to plead it because he is righteous. As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation — the wrath of God against our sin has been absorbed at the cross. These are not two separate acts but two perspectives on the one act of the cross. The same sacrifice that satisfied divine justice now grounds our ongoing access to divine mercy. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is both objective (propitiation — something accomplished outside us, in history, on a cross) and applied (advocacy — an ongoing ministry of Christ on our behalf). Both are necessary; together they produce the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John's three tests — obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11), and belief (2:22–23) — are not a checklist for earning assurance but symptoms of new birth. Just as a doctor looks for signs of life, John looks for the signs that genuine regeneration has occurred. These tests are not meant to produce anxiety but clarity: not "have I been good enough?" but "is there genuine fruit of the Spirit in my life?" The tests are cumulative and mutually reinforcing — genuine obedience produces love; genuine love flows from right belief; genuine belief manifests in how we treat the brothers and sisters.
2.examples:
Then: The antichrists who had left the community had claimed a superior knowledge of God. Their departure seemed, to some, like the enlightened ones leaving the unenlightened behind. John's response is pastoral and pointed: the ones who left proved by their leaving that they were never truly of the community (2:19). This is not cruelty but theology — genuine new birth produces perseverance. The ones who remained, confused and perhaps diminished, were the ones who had "the anointing from the Holy One" and knew the truth (2:20). The test of authenticity is not sophistication but faithfulness to the beginning.

Now: We live in a world of novelty — new spiritualities, new therapies, new paths to self-actualization. The church is perpetually tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more culturally current, more psychologically satisfying, more intellectually respectable. John's word is the same: let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. The gospel does not need to be updated; it needs to be inhabited. The depth we seek is not found by moving beyond the cross — it is found by going deeper into it.

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.<sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.<sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.<sup>4</sup>Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.<sup>5</sup>You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.<sup>6</sup>No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.<sup>7</sup>Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.<sup>8</sup>Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.<sup>9</sup>No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.<sup>10</sup>By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.<sup>11</sup>For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.<sup>12</sup>We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.<sup>13</sup>Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.<sup>14</sup>We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.<sup>15</sup>Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.<sup>16</sup>By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.<sup>17</sup>But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?<sup>18</sup>Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.<sup>19</sup>By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him;<sup>20</sup>for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.<sup>21</sup>Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;<sup>22</sup>and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.<sup>23</sup>And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.<sup>24</sup>Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens in wonder: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are.” We are God’s children now, and when Christ appears we shall be like him. That hope makes us pure.

Then John shows what God’s children look like. They do not live in sin, because God’s seed abides in them and the Son came to destroy the devil’s works. And they love one another, not in words only, but in deeds, as Christ laid down his life for us. When the heart condemns, God is greater than our heart. His command is to believe in his Son and love one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Children of God: Now and Not Yet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John commands us to look: “See what kind of love”. The phrase suggests something foreign and astonishing. God calls us his children, “and so we are”. The world does not recognise us, because it did not recognise him. We are children now; what we will be is not yet seen. But when Christ appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. And everyone with that hope purifies himself now.
verseByVerse.theology:
Children Now, Like Him Then

We are God’s children now; when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. That hope purifies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some claimed they had already arrived.

Now: We become what we behold; set your hope on his appearing.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at the astonishing love the Father has shown: he calls us his children, and that is what we really are. The world does not recognise us because it did not recognise him.

What kind of love. The word (potapēn) was used by the disciples of the man whom wind and sea obeyed (Matthew 8:27). This love comes from outside our world.

“And so we are.” Not a courtesy title, but a fact. The holy God has adopted rebels into his family.

On a Tuesday. You fail at work, or feel invisible at a party, or are laughed at for your faith. Before anything else, remember what you are: a child of the Father, loved with a love from another world. Let that move you to worship before it moves you to anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are God’s children now. What we will become has not yet been revealed, but we know that when Christ appears we will be like him, because we will see him as he really is.

Now and not yet. We are already children; the full glory of it is still hidden.

Seeing makes us like him. The vision of Christ produces the likeness. What a lifetime of sanctification has been moving towards, seeing him will complete in a moment.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who has this hope in Christ purifies himself, just as Christ is pure.

Hope that works. Real hope in Christ’s return pulls the future into the present. The standard is his own purity.

What it does not mean. It is not achieved sinlessness, which 1:8 rules out. It is the direction of a life that is being shaped towards the one it hopes to see.

On a Tuesday. A bride getting ready for her wedding does not need to be told to take care of her dress. Hope shapes behaviour. So does the hope of meeting Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Sin, the Devil, and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This passage must be read carefully, or it will either terrify the true believer or comfort the false one. John speaks of two families, known by how they live. The devil has sinned from the beginning; the Son of God appeared to destroy his works. God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives. John is not teaching sinless perfection (1:8–10), but that the new birth changes the direction of a life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Birth

The Son appeared to take away sins and to destroy the works of the devil. God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Claimed spiritual knowledge was being used to excuse sin.

Now: Avoid both errors: tolerating sin as normal, and thinking that any sin proves you are not born again.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who lives in sin lives in lawlessness, because sin is lawlessness.

What sin is. At heart, sin is rebellion against God’s authority, not just breaking social rules or a psychological problem. Every sin, however small, shares in that rebellion.

verseByVerse.quote: You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ appeared to take away sins, and there is no sin in him.

Why he came. The cross was not an afterthought; it was the mission. “Take away” means to lift and carry off (John 1:29).

Sinless. Only the one with no sin could bear the sins of others. Christ’s sinlessness is the foundation of the atonement.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who lives in Christ goes on living in sin, and no one who goes on living in sin has truly seen or known him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a true Christian never sins. John has just said that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself (1:8), and he has given the remedy for sin (2:1). He means a settled, unrepentant pattern of sin.

A note on grammar. The ESV’s “keeps on sinning” reflects the Greek present tense. But tense alone does not prove a habit; that is a common exegetical fallacy. What makes it clear is the context: John has already told believers they will sin and must confess. The contrast is between a life that fights sin and a life at peace with it.

On a Tuesday. A believer who has fallen again into the same sin wonders whether she was ever a Christian. Her grief over it, and her running back to Christ, are signs of new life. The person John warns about is the one who sins and no longer cares.
verseByVerse.note: The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse (compare 1:8–2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived: whoever does what is right is righteous, just as Christ is righteous.

Evidence, not cause. We do not become righteous by doing right; we do right because God has made us righteous in Christ. But that gift always shows itself. The false teachers offered a spirituality without a matching life. John will not allow the split.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever lives in sin belongs to the devil, who has sinned from the start. But the Son of God came to destroy the devil’s works.

Two families. A life given over to sin bears the family likeness of the devil.

Destroy. The verb means to undo, dismantle, loosen. Christ entered the territory the devil thought he owned and began taking his works apart: sin’s power, death’s reign, the accuser’s hold. The outcome is not in doubt.

On a Tuesday. A habit has held you for years and you feel it will never break. The Son of God appeared to destroy precisely this kind of thing. Fight it in his strength, and praise him for every inch he wins.

verseByVerse.quote: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one born of God lives in sin, because God’s seed remains in him. He cannot go on sinning, because he is born of God.

God’s seed. The new birth implants God’s own life, which goes on working. That life is at war with sin and pulls towards God.

“Cannot”. Not that the believer is unable to commit a sin, but that he cannot settle into sin as his way of life. Sin in a Christian is always out of place, resisted and confessed.

A wrong view. Some teach that believers can reach a state where they no longer sin. John’s own words exclude it (1:8, 10). Others treat sin in Christians as normal and harmless. John excludes that too.

verseByVerse.quote: By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is how God’s children and the devil’s children are recognised: anyone who does not do right, or who does not love his brother, is not from God.

No neutral ground. Behind every life is a spiritual parentage, revealed by its direction. The two signs, righteousness and love, belong together, and the next verses develop the second.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — Love One Another: The Cain Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John brings love down to earth: the brother in front of you. He starts with Cain, who hated and murdered his brother because Abel was righteous. That is why the world hates believers. Then comes the clearest definition of love in the New Testament: “By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us.” The cross defines love, and obliges us to love the same way, starting with an open hand to a brother in need.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love Defined by the Cross

Cain hated his brother; Christ laid down his life for us. By this we know love, and we ought to lay down our lives for one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The world’s hatred was not to surprise the church.

Now: Love in deed and truth: an open hand to a brother in need.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message they heard from the beginning is this: love one another.

Not advanced teaching. Love is not an optional extra for the mature. It is the apostolic message itself, and what the gospel produces in those who receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother, because his own actions were evil and his brother’s were righteous.

Why Cain killed. Abel’s righteousness exposed Cain’s evil. Goodness does not need to speak to accuse; its presence is enough. That is why the world often resents faithful believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be surprised that the world hates you.

Expect it. Jesus said it would happen (John 15:18–19). It is not a sign that God is displeased or that you have failed. The right response is not retaliation, not compromise and not self-pity, but steady faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know we have passed from death to life because we love our fellow believers. Whoever does not love remains in death.

Evidence of life. Love for other Christians is not just a nice trait; it is a fingerprint of the new birth. We crossed from death to life, and the love that now marks us shows it.

On a Tuesday. You doubt your salvation. Ask: do I love God’s people? Do I want to be with them, help them, forgive them? If so, that love is evidence of the Spirit’s work. Thank God for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and no murderer has eternal life living in him.

Murder in the heart. John echoes Jesus (Matthew 5:21–22): hatred is murder at the root.

What it does not mean. It is not a threat against a believer who feels anger and fights it. It describes a life marked by settled, unrepented hatred.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know what love is because Christ gave his life for us, and so we ought to give our lives for one another.

The cross defines love. We do not bring our own idea of love to the cross. The cross teaches us what love is.

We owe it. “Ought” means we are in debt. The same verb John uses for Christ laying down his life is now applied to us.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If someone has material possessions and sees a fellow believer in need but refuses to help, how can God’s love be in him?

The concrete test. Not martyrdom, which may never be asked, but the need you can see, with resources you have. “Closes his heart” pictures shutting off compassion on purpose.

On a Tuesday. A family in your church has lost an income. You hear about it and feel sorry for them. John asks what you will do. Love may look like a bag of shopping, a quiet gift, or an evening babysitting so they can rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not love only with words, but with actions and in truth.

Deed and truth. Kind words are not enough, and can deceive us into thinking we have loved. Real love does something, and does it sincerely, not for applause. John includes himself: “let us”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — Assurance, Prayer, and the Mutual Indwelling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After such a demanding call to love, the question follows: what if I have not loved enough? What if my heart condemns me? John answers tenderly: God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything. Then comes the freedom of prayer, and a summary of the whole Christian life: believe in the name of God’s Son, and love one another. The Spirit he has given assures us that he lives in us.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Greater than Our Heart

When our heart condemns us, God is greater and knows everything. His commandment is to believe in his Son and to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Assurance rested on love in deed and on the Spirit given to them.

Now: A tender conscience can rest in God’s fuller knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Loving in deed and truth shows that we belong to the truth and lets us reassure our hearts before God, because whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart and knows everything.

Two readings. Some read “God is greater than our heart” as a warning: if our conscience condemns us, God, who knows even more, condemns us more. Most read it as comfort, and the context supports that: John is reassuring the heart. God’s knowledge of us is truer than our own. He sees faith beneath the failures and real love in imperfect deeds.

On a Tuesday. A sensitive believer lies awake, sure she has failed God beyond repair. Her heart condemns her. John tells her to look past her heart to God, who knows everything, including the blood of his Son and the love he has put in her. She can rest there.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God.

Boldness. The word (parrēsia) means open-faced freedom. A peaceful conscience is not proof of perfection, but a gift that frees us to approach God without cringing.

verseByVerse.quote: and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We receive whatever we ask from him, because we keep his commands and do what pleases him.

What it does not mean. It is not a transaction where obedience unlocks answers, nor a promise of anything we fancy. Those who live to please God increasingly ask for what pleases him, and he is glad to give it (5:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s command is that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another.

One command. John uses the singular. Faith and love are two sides of one response: real faith in Christ always produces love, and real Christian love is always rooted in faith in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps God’s commands lives in God, and God in him. We know that he lives in us by the Spirit he has given us.

Mutual indwelling. The believer is in God, and God in the believer, the closest union there is (John 15:4).

The Spirit’s witness. We know this by the Spirit, who produces love, testifies that we are God’s children (Romans 8:16), and keeps us in the truth. Assurance rests finally not on our feelings, but on God’s gift.

3.theology:
Adoption and Transformation. The doctrine of adoption is one of the richest in the New Testament, and 3:1–3, with its language of being born of God and called his children, is one of its highest expressions. To be called children of God is not a metaphor of religious devotion; it is a declaration of a new ontological status. We have been brought into the family of God — not as servants, not as subjects, but as children who share in the inheritance of the Son. And adoption in John is both present reality ("so we are," v.1) and future consummation ("what we will be has not yet appeared," v.2). The "not yet" of our glorification does not undermine the "already" of our adoption; the hope of the appearing purifies the life of the one who holds it.

Love Defined by the Cross. John's definition of love in verse 16 is one of the most consequential sentences in the New Testament. He does not say "God is love, therefore love is whatever feels loving." He says love is defined by a specific act: the laying down of the life of the Son. The cross is love's definition, love's measure, and love's demand. Reformed theology has always insisted that the love of God is not sentimentality but holy self-giving at infinite cost. Every theology of love that avoids the cross will eventually become a theology of tolerance — and tolerance is not love. Love is the cross, and the cross makes demands.
3.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had experienced the pain of betrayal — people they had loved had left. The temptation in such a situation is to turn inward, to protect the heart, to love in word only and keep the real self safely guarded. John's word to them is the cross: he laid down his life. Not as an inspiration to imitate from a safe distance, but as the very definition and pattern of what love is. The ones who remained in the fellowship were called to love one another with an openness that made them vulnerable — precisely because that is what love, defined by the cross, requires.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that defines love primarily as acceptance and validation. John defines it as sacrifice. The question is not "do I feel warmly toward my brother?" but "am I laying anything down for my brother?" The test of love is not interior but behavioural — not word and talk but deed and truth. A closed hand toward a brother in need, whatever feelings accompany it, is not love in John's sense. The cross makes love costly, specific, and concrete.

4.title: Testing the Spirits and the Love of God
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.<sup>2</sup>By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God,<sup>3</sup>and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.<sup>4</sup>Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.<sup>5</sup>They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.<sup>6</sup>We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.<sup>8</sup>Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.<sup>9</sup>In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.<sup>10</sup>In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.<sup>11</sup>Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.<sup>12</sup>No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.<sup>13</sup>By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.<sup>14</sup>And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.<sup>15</sup>Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.<sup>16</sup>So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.<sup>17</sup>By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.<sup>18</sup>There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.<sup>19</sup>We love because he first loved us.<sup>20</sup>If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.<sup>21</sup>And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 begins with a warning and rises to the fullest teaching on the love of God in the New Testament. The warning: test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out. The test is whether a teaching confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Then John says twice, “God is love” (vv. 8, 16). He never lets this become vague. God’s love is defined by its greatest act: he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. That love casts out the fear of punishment, and it flows on through us to one another: “We love because he first loved us.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Testing the Spirits: Discernment in the Last Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits.” Not every teaching that claims to come from God does. False prophets rarely announce themselves; they use Christian words with spiritual intensity. John’s test goes to the heart of the gospel: does the teaching confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? And he ends with confidence: “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing the Spirits

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: False prophets had gone out into the world.

Now: Ask of any teaching whether it confesses the whole Christ — truly God, truly man, crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not believe every spiritual claim, but test whether it comes from God, because many false prophets are at work in the world.

A duty for all. The command is to the whole church, not only its leaders. Discernment is every believer’s responsibility.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suspicion of everyone, or refusing to learn from teachers. It means weighing what we hear against the apostolic gospel, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11).

verseByVerse.quote: By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is how to recognise God’s Spirit: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. That is the spirit of antichrist, already in the world.

The test. Does it confess the real incarnation, the eternal Son truly and permanently become man? A teaching that separates the divine Christ from the human Jesus, or treats his body as a costume, fails.

A textual note. In v. 3 a few early writers and the Latin Vulgate read “every spirit that dissolves (or divides) Jesus”. Almost all Greek manuscripts read “does not confess Jesus”, and that is very likely original. The variant, though, shows how early readers understood the error: dividing Jesus from the Christ.

On a Tuesday. A popular spiritual book says that “the Christ” is a universal consciousness that Jesus happened to discover. It sounds deep. John’s test is simple: is Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen, confessed as the Christ come in the flesh? If not, put the book down.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You belong to God and have defeated the false prophets, because the Spirit who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.

Already overcome. John does not leave the church anxious. The victory has already happened. Its ground is not their cleverness but the one who lives in them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers cannot be deceived, or need not watch; John has just told them to test. It means they need not fear. The weakest believer carries a greater power than the spirit behind every false teacher.
