verseByVerse.quote: They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false prophets belong to the world, so they speak the world’s language, and the world listens to them.

Popularity is no proof. They are shaped by what the world finds respectable and comforting, so the world welcomes them. When a message is warmly received by people who have no interest in Christ, it is worth testing all the more.

verseByVerse.quote: We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles belong to God. Whoever knows God listens to them; whoever does not belong to God does not. This is how to tell the Spirit of truth from the spirit of error.

The apostolic word. John speaks as an apostle. Those who know God recognise and receive the apostolic teaching, as sheep know their shepherd’s voice (John 10:4). Today that means receiving the New Testament as God’s word.

Two tests together. The content of the confession (vv. 2–3) and a Spirit-given recognition of the apostolic word go together. Neither stands alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — God Is Love: The Source, the Measure, and the Goal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “God is love.” John does not mean a warm feeling or a tolerant mood. Love is the life the Father, Son and Spirit have shared from eternity. And this love has been shown: God sent his only Son so that we might live through him, as the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we ought to love one another. And when we do, the invisible God is seen in his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Love

Love is from God, and God showed it by sending his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The departing teachers’ knowledge produced schism, not love.

Now: No one has ever seen God; when we love one another, his love is made complete in us.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us love one another, because love comes from God, and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows him.

Love from God. Christian love does not start in our natural kindness. It flows from God, and it shows that we have been born of him.

Doctrine and love. John moves straight from testing doctrine to love. They are not alternatives for different temperaments, but one life.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.

God is love. Not only that God is loving, but that love is what he is: the Father loving the Son and the Son the Father in the Spirit, before there was any world. To know such a God and remain unloving is impossible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there is no hell, or that God will condemn no one. John has also said, “God is light” (1:5). And he defines love by the cross: God “sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (v. 10). Propitiation means turning away wrath. God’s love does not cancel his justice; it satisfies it at infinite cost. Nor does it mean that “love is God”, so that every human love is divine. John defines love by God, not God by our ideas of love.

verseByVerse.quote: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God showed his love by sending his one and only Son into the world, so that we might have life through him.

A real event. Love is not just an idea. It happened: God sent his only Son. “Only” (monogenēs) shows the cost: not one messenger among many, but the unique Son.

Life for the dead. Without Christ we are spiritually dead (Ephesians 2:1). God’s love comes down into our death and brings life.

verseByVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Real love is not our love for God, but his love for us, shown in sending his Son to be the sacrifice that turns away his wrath against our sins.

The direction of love. It runs from God to us. We did not start it. We were loved before we loved.

Propitiation. The Son bore the penalty God’s holiness required, so that sinners could be welcomed without justice being set aside.

On a Tuesday. On days when your love for God feels thin, do not start with your love. Start here: he loved you and sent his Son. Your love will grow as you look at his.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since God loved us so much, we too ought to love one another.

Obligation and power. “If” means “since”. Those loved at such cost have no right to withhold love. And God’s love, poured into our hearts by the Spirit (Romans 5:5), is not only a model to copy but a power to draw on.

verseByVerse.quote: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ever seen God, but if we love one another, God lives in us and his love is brought to completion in us.

God seen in his people. The invisible God becomes visible when his people love each other across every difference. His love reaches its goal when it flows through us to others.

On a Tuesday. A church where wealthy and poor, old and young, sit together, eat together and care for one another shows the world something no argument can. Your small act of love this week is part of that picture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Abiding in Love: Confidence, Fear Cast Out, and the Visible Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Assurance rests on the Spirit God has given (v. 13) and the confession of his Son (v. 15). From that union comes confidence even for the day of judgment, because “as he is so also are we in this world.” Perfect love casts out the fear of punishment. And love for the invisible God is tested by love for the brother we can see.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear Cast Out

Those who abide in love have confidence for the day of judgement. Perfect love casts out fear, and we love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Confidence rested on union with the Son, not on claimed knowledge.

Now: The brother we can see tests our love for the God we cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that we live in God and he in us because he has given us his Spirit.

The Spirit’s witness. We do not deduce our union with God from our achievements or feelings. God has given us his Spirit, who testifies that we are his children (Romans 8:16), produces love and keeps us confessing Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son to be the Saviour of the world.

Eyewitnesses. John again rests his message on what was seen.

What it does not mean. “Saviour of the world” does not mean that every person will be saved. It means that Christ is not a tribal or national saviour, but the only Saviour for people of every nation, and fully able to save all who come to him (John 4:42).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God has God living in him, and he lives in God.

Confession. Confessing Jesus as God’s Son is not a work that earns union with God. It is the open hand of faith that receives it.

verseByVerse.quote: So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have come to know and believe the love God has for us. God is love, and whoever lives in love lives in God, and God in him.

Know and believe. Both: understanding God’s love and trusting it.

Living in love. Love is not something we add to our relationship with God. It is the atmosphere in which God dwells. Where real, Christ-shaped love is, God is.

verseByVerse.quote: By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is made complete among us so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because in this world we are like Christ.

Confidence for judgment day. The ground is not our moral record but our union with Christ. “As he is”, not as he was: the risen, vindicated Son, in whom we are hidden (Colossians 3:3). The judgment we deserved, he bore. His verdict, “beloved Son”, is shared with those in him.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no fear in love; perfect love drives out fear, because fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been made complete in love.

Which fear? The fear of punishment: the dread of a slave who expects a beating.

What it does not mean. It does not abolish the fear of the Lord. Scripture calls believers to reverent awe before God (Proverbs 1:7; Hebrews 12:28–29; 1 Peter 1:17). That holy fear is not the opposite of love but its companion. The more we grasp God’s love at the cross, the more we tremble at his holiness, and the less we fear his condemnation.

On a Tuesday. A believer who still lives in dread of God’s anger does not need to try harder. He needs to look longer at the cross, where the punishment was borne. Then he will fear God as a child reveres a holy Father, not as a criminal fears a judge.

verseByVerse.quote: We love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We love because God loved us first.

The whole gospel in brief. God’s love came first; ours is the response. We do not love in order to be loved, but because we are already loved.

A textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “We love him”. The earlier and better manuscripts simply read “We love”. The shorter reading is more likely original, and it is broader: God’s love produces our love for him and for others.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who says he loves God but hates his brother is a liar, because if he does not love the brother he can see, he cannot love God whom he has not seen.

The visible test. It is easy to claim love for an invisible God. The test is the actual person in front of you, with all their faults.

On a Tuesday. You love worship on Sunday but avoid the member who annoys you. John says the two cannot be separated. Pray for that person by name, and look for one way to do them good this week.

verseByVerse.quote: And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has commanded that whoever loves him must also love his brother.

One command. Love for God and love for his children are not two duties to balance, but one obedience. The chapter began with testing the spirits and ends with love: the Spirit of truth always produces love, and the spirit of error, sooner or later, produces division.

4.theology:
God is Love. The statement "God is love" (vv. 8, 16) is one of the most misused sentences in Scripture. It is taken to mean that love is God — that whatever we call love must be divine, that God must approve of whatever we name as love. John means the opposite: God defines love, not the other way around. And he defines it immediately by a specific act: the sending of the Son to be the propitiation. To say "God is love" in John's sense is to say that God, in his innermost being, is the kind of God who sends his only Son into the world to die for sinners who could not save themselves. That is the love John is talking about. It is not soft; it is costly. It is not tolerant; it is propitiatory. It is not vague; it has flesh and blood and a cross and an empty tomb.

The Expulsion of Fear. The pastoral application of the doctrine of propitiation in verses 17–18 is one of the most comforting passages in the New Testament. The believer who is tortured by fear of God's judgment has not yet fully grasped what the propitiation means: that the very wrath they fear has been exhausted, absorbed, satisfied in the beloved Son. Perfect love casts out fear not by denying the reality of judgment but by pointing to the one who bore it. Reformed theology speaks of the "double jeopardy" of the cross: it would be unjust for God to punish twice what Christ has already borne. The blood of Jesus is the answer to every accusing conscience, every fear of condemnation, every midnight terror of a soul that wonders whether it is safe with God.
4.examples:
Then: The community had been shaken by teachers who claimed spiritual authority and offered a more sophisticated understanding of God. The test John gives is arrestingly simple: do they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? Not "do they seem spiritual?" Not "do they have impressive experiences?" But: do they hold to the incarnation? This is always the fault line. Every theological error that has ever devastated a church has at some point compromised either the full deity or the full humanity of Christ. John's readers are given a test simple enough for a child and decisive enough to unmask every false spirit.

Now: "We love because he first loved us" is the answer to every form of Christian guilt and striving. The Christian life is not a performance of love in order to earn God's approval; it is a response of love to a love already given, already completed, already victorious at the cross. When love runs dry — as it will — the answer is not to try harder but to go back to the source: "In this is love, not that we have loved God..." The spring of all Christian love is the love of God in the cross of his Son. Drink there again, and love will flow.

5.title: Faith that Overcomes, Life that is Sure
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.<sup>2</sup>By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.<sup>3</sup>For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.<sup>4</sup>For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.<sup>5</sup>Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?<sup>6</sup>This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.<sup>7</sup>For there are three that testify:<sup>8</sup>the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.<sup>9</sup>If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.<sup>10</sup>Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. 5.overview:
The final chapter of 1 John brings the letter to its great crescendo. The three tests — belief, love, obedience — converge in a single declaration: everyone born of God overcomes the world, and the victory is faith. Not faith as a heroic human achievement, but faith as the empty hand that receives the Son of God — and in receiving the Son, receives life itself. "Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life." The whole letter has been building to this clarity: salvation is not a process, not a feeling, not a spiritual achievement. It is a person. To have the Son is to have life. To be without the Son is to be without life. There is no middle ground.

And then, the stated purpose of the letter, which makes it the most explicitly pastoral book in the New Testament: "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life." Not that you may hope, or that you may feel, or that you may occasionally experience. That you may know. The epistle of assurance reaches its goal: settled, humble, grateful certainty in the hearts of those who have the Son. The letter closes with the most luminous declaration of all — "This is the true God and eternal life" — Jesus Christ himself, the content of the eternal life that John has been proclaiming from the beginning, the one who was with the Father and was manifested to us, in whom and through whom and for whom all things are.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Faith, Love, and the World-Overcoming Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John opens the final chapter of his letter by drawing together the three threads that have run through it from the beginning: faith, new birth, and love. They are not separate themes that happen to appear in the same letter; they are facets of a single reality. Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God — belief and new birth are inseparable. And whoever has been born of God loves the Father and loves those born of the Father — new birth and love are inseparable. The ethical command to love the brothers (which has dominated chapters 3–4) is now grounded in the new birth, which itself issues in faith. The cascade is complete: birth produces faith, birth produces love, and love proves the birth.

And then the chapter delivers one of the most stirring affirmations in the New Testament: everyone born of God overcomes the world. Not struggles against the world, not occasionally resists the world, not tries very hard to avoid the world — overcomes it. The victory has already been achieved in Christ (Jn 16:33), and the believer participates in that victory through faith. The world — the age organised against God, with all its powers, seductions, and hostilities — has been defeated by the one in whom we believe, and our faith is the means by which his victory becomes ours. The question that closes the section cuts through everything: who overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? There is only one answer, and the whole epistle has been pointing toward it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as the Victory

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God and loves God’s children. Faith in the Son of God overcomes the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ordinary faith was being called insufficient.

Now: His commandments are not burdensome where love for him is real.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The three great themes of the epistle — faith, new birth, and love — are bound together in a single verse. Believing that Jesus is the Christ is inseparable from the new birth: the faith is the evidence of the birth, and the birth is the source of the faith. Then the logic extends horizontally: whoever loves the Father loves those born of the Father. Family love is not optional for those who genuinely love the head of the family; the love naturally extends to all who bear the family likeness. This verse is the hinge between chapters 4 and 5, connecting the love-command of ch. 4 with the assurance and victory of ch. 5, by grounding both in the new birth, which produces faith.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary: The test runs in a direction that might seem counterintuitive: we know we love the children of God by loving God and obeying his commandments. In 4:20, love for the visible brother tested love for the invisible God; here love for the invisible God measures love for the visible community. The two tests are complementary, not contradictory. Love for God (the vertical) expresses itself in obedience to his commandments, which include the command to love the brothers. There is no genuinely God-oriented obedience that excludes love for the community; and there is no genuinely community-oriented love that excludes obedience to God. The two are indissoluble.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.
verseByVerse.commentary: Love for God is defined not as a feeling toward him but as obedience to his commandments — the thoroughly Johannine and thoroughly Hebrew equation (Jn 14:15; Deut 6:5 + 11:22). And then the liberating word: his commandments are not burdensome. The Greek bareiai means heavy, oppressive, crushing. The law of God, for the one born of God and indwelt by the Spirit, is not a crushing external obligation but the natural expression of a new nature. The new birth creates the capacity to delight in what God commands (Ps 119:35; Rom 7:22). Where obedience feels like nothing but grinding burden, the diagnostic question is not “how do I try harder?” but “is the love of God real and growing in me?”

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: One of the most confident declarations in the letter. The born-of-God believer does not merely resist the world or avoid it; overcomes it. The phrase "the victory that has overcome" looks back to the decisive defeat of the world-system in Christ’s death and resurrection (Jn 16:33, “I have overcome the world”). Our faith is the means of participation in that already-accomplished victory — the hand that reaches out and holds the one who has already won. We do not overcome the world by moral accumulation or spiritual discipline alone, though both matter; we overcome it by trusting the one who has already overcome it, and thereby sharing in his conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?
verseByVerse.commentary: The rhetorical question has exactly one answer. The faith that overcomes the world is specifically faith in Jesus as the Son of God — the full christological identity established throughout the epistle. Not a generic spirituality, not trust in a divine principle, not confidence in one’s own spiritual resources, but faith in this person, with this specific identity, doing this specific work. The confession of Jesus as Son of God (4:15) is not a theological luxury that can be softened for a wider audience; it is the decisive thing that determines whether the life is genuinely connected to the source of world-overcoming power. The question is exclusive by design and inclusive by invitation: anyone who believes this overcomes; no one who refuses it does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Three Witnesses and the Life That Is in the Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This section addresses what is perhaps the most technically difficult passage in the epistle, and it does so for a pastoral reason: the false teaching that threatened John’s community was striking at the very identity of Jesus, and John is providing the court-level evidence for who Jesus is. In Jewish law, a matter is established by two or three witnesses (Deut 19:15); God provides three: the Spirit, the water, and the blood. The Spirit testifies because the Spirit is truth; the water and the blood are the historical bookends of Jesus’s ministry — his baptism and his death — which together declare the full identity and mission of the Christ.

And God’s own testimony about his Son is greater than any human testimony: if we accept the word of human witnesses in courts of law and scientific laboratories, how much more should we accept the testimony of the one who cannot lie? The believer has this testimony within them — the Spirit’s internal witness confirming the external word. And the content of that testimony is the most compact and the most comprehensive statement of the gospel in the letter: God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life. There is no middle position, no partial possession, no probationary category: the Son is present or absent, and life follows the Son without remainder or exception.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Three Witnesses

The Spirit, the water and the blood agree: the one who was baptised is the one who died. God has given eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teaching separated the Christ of the baptism from the Jesus of the cross.

Now: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most exegetically debated verse in the chapter. The most likely reading: “water” refers to the baptism of Jesus and “blood” to his crucifixion — the two public events that together mark the beginning and end of his public ministry and together declare his full identity and mission. The false teaching John opposed seems to have held that the divine Christ descended at the baptism but departed before the cross, leaving only the human Jesus to die. John’s insistence is emphatic: he came not by the water only but by the water and the blood. The same person was baptised and crucified; the divine and the human were not separated. And the Spirit, who is truth itself, bears witness to this full identity — not to a divided Christ but to the one Jesus Christ who is both.

What do water and blood mean? Some take them as the water and blood that flowed from Jesus’ side (John 19:34); others as baptism and the Lord’s Supper. The more likely reading is that the water is Jesus’ baptism, where his ministry began, and the blood his death: the false teachers said the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross, and John insists that the Son of God came not by the water only but by the water and the blood.
verseByVerse.note: “Water and blood” probably refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death — against teachers who said the divine Christ left Jesus before the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are three that testify: the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three witnesses — the Spirit, the water, and the blood — give unanimous testimony to the full identity of Jesus Christ. The legal background is Deuteronomy 19:15: a matter is established by two or three witnesses. God provides three, and they agree — are in harmony, speak with one voice. The Spirit’s testimony is the internal, ongoing witness given to believers (v. 10; 4:13); the water and the blood are the historical events of Jesus’s ministry that publicly declared his identity at its beginning and at its completion. The convergence of these three witnesses on the one Jesus Christ is not accidental but providential: God has ensured that the testimony to his Son is abundant, consistent, and legally sufficient. Those who deny it are not lacking evidence; they are suppressing it.

One note for readers using the King James Version, which carries extra words here — the so-called Comma Johanneum: ‘the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.’ However true that statement is in itself, it is almost certainly not part of what John wrote. It is missing from virtually every Greek manuscript and surfaces only in late Latin copies — apparently a marginal note that later crept into the text. Nothing is lost by its absence: the doctrine of the Trinity rests on the whole of Scripture and never depended on this one line, and the three witnesses John actually gave — Spirit, water, and blood — supply all the testimony his argument needs.
verseByVerse.note: Some late manuscripts add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven (known from the King James Version). They are not in the early Greek manuscripts and the ESV omits them.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary: An argument from the lesser to the greater. Human testimony is received every day as adequate grounds for belief — in courtrooms, in history books, in medical diagnoses. We structure entire civilisations on the reliability of credible human witnesses. The testimony of God is categorically greater, being the word of the one who is truth itself, who cannot be deceived and cannot deceive. And God has borne testimony concerning his Son — at the baptism (“This is my beloved Son,” Matt 3:17), through the resurrection (Rom 1:4), through the gift of the Spirit (Jn 15:26–27), and through the internal witness of vv. 7–8. To receive human testimony and refuse divine testimony is not sceptical caution; it is a moral and epistemic inconsistency that John will name plainly in v. 10.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit’s internal witness is the believer’s own possession: the one who believes “has the testimony in himself” — the Spirit bears witness with our spirit (Rom 8:16), confirming the apostolic testimony as true within the believer’s own experience of new life. This is not private subjectivism; it is the objective testimony of the Spirit given within the subjective experience of the believer. The converse is sobering: the one who does not believe makes God a liar. This is not hyperbole. To receive a witness’s testimony, hear it clearly, and then refuse it is not a neutral act of intellectual caution; it is an active impugning of the witness’s truthfulness. Unbelief in the gospel is not merely a spiritual problem; it is an act of cosmic slander against the God who testified.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary: The content of God’s testimony about his Son, stated with the precision and economy of a creedal formula: God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Two truths held together. First, the gift: God gave — past tense, already accomplished, already given, requiring only reception. Second, the location: the life is in the Son. Eternal life is not a commodity distributed independently of Christ; it is a person-located reality. This is why “having the Son” (v. 12) and “having life” are the same thing: to be in Christ is to have the life; to be outside Christ is to be outside the life. No formula, no ritual, no spiritual discipline, no religious achievement can transfer the life apart from the Son in whom it resides.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The starkest binary in the epistle and one of the sharpest in the New Testament. Not “more or less life” depending on spiritual development; not “life of different quality” depending on doctrinal precision — has or does not have, life or not life. The Son is either possessed (by faith, in union) or he is not, and life follows the Son without remainder. This is both the most inclusive possible invitation (anyone, from any background, may have the Son by faith) and the most exclusive possible statement (no other means of possessing life exists). To soften this binary is not pastoral generosity but a failure of love: it leaves people comfortable in a condition John has just described as the absence of life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Knowing What We Have in Christ: Assurance, Prayer, and the True God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John states the purpose of the epistle in v. 13 with a simplicity that should stop us in our tracks: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life. Not hope, not suspect, not feel on good days — know. The whole letter has been building toward this confidence, providing the tests by which the genuine believer may be assured of what they have. And now the assured believer is shown what they may do with their assurance: pray with boldness (vv. 14–15), intercede for sinning brothers (vv. 16–17), and live in the certainty of three great “we know” truths that the letter has been establishing. We know that the one born of God does not keep on sinning — the new birth is real and its effects are real.

We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the evil one — we live in hostile territory, but we are not of it. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true — the great circle closes. The letter that opened with eyewitness testimony to the eternal Word made touchable ends with the declaration that this Word has come, has given us minds and hearts to know the true God, and is himself the true God and eternal life. The last command — little children, keep yourselves from idols — is not an afterthought; it is the practical corollary of everything that has come before. You have the true God. Do not settle for anything less.
verseByVerse.theology:
That You May Know

John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life. They may pray with confidence, intercede for a sinning brother, and rest in what they know.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The letter closes on Jesus Christ as the true God and eternal life.

Now: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The stated purpose of the entire letter. John writes not to evangelise but to assure — his audience already believes, and what they need is confidence in what believing gives them. That you may know — not hope, not feel, not reasonably expect — know — with the certainty of direct perception. The knowledge John offers is not the hidden mystical knowledge of the opponents; it is the plain, testable, Spirit-confirmed knowledge that comes from believing in the name of the Son of God and living the life the epistle has described. Assurance is not presumption; it is the appropriate response to the reliability of God’s word about his Son.
verseByVerse.note: John’s Gospel was written that readers might believe; this letter that believers might know they have eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The assured believer of v. 13 immediately has a posture toward God in prayer: parrēsia — bold, open, unashamed confidence. The condition of answered prayer — according to his will — is not a limiting clause designed to lower expectations but a clarifying one: prayer aligned with God’s will is prayer that will certainly be heard. The shift this produces is from “will God hear me?” (anxious petitioning) to “what is God’s will?” (collaborative alignment). The person who knows God through his word and Spirit can pray with confidence not because they have mastered a formula but because they are asking in the direction God is already moving.

verseByVerse.quote: And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The logic of v. 14 pressed to its conclusion: if God hears (v. 14), the requests are granted. “We have the requests” is striking — not “we will have” but “we have,” even before the visible answer appears. This is the confidence of faith that takes God at his word: the one who has asked according to his will can live in the certainty of the answer because God’s hearing is itself the act of granting. This is not a blank cheque for any desire labelled “prayer”; it is the confident posture of the person whose asking has been shaped by the God they know.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most exegetically contested passage in the letter. The confident intercession of vv. 14–15 is immediately applied to the most painful of pastoral situations: a sinning brother. John commands intercession for the brother committing sin “not leading to death” — most likely the ordinary failures and sins of genuine believers, for which repentance and forgiveness remain available (1:9). “Sin leading to death” is most likely the settled, unrepentant denial of Christ by those who have definitively left the community (2:19; 4:2–3) — the final, hardened apostasy. John does not forbid prayer for such persons but does not command it, recognising a possible point of no return. The positive pastoral point stands: when you see a struggling brother, intercede. God gives life through the prayers of the community.

Others have read ‘sin leading to death’ differently — as the unpardonable sin of blaspheming the Spirit (Matt 12:31–32), or as physical death under God’s hand of discipline (as with Ananias and Sapphira, Acts 5:1–11) — and the honest truth is that we cannot be dogmatic about which John meant. But whichever way it is read, his refusal to command prayer ‘for that’ is not a ban on interceding; it is pastoral honesty, for a prayer for restoration assumes the person can still be restored. And the main point is not swallowed up by the hard exception: when you see a brother struggling and falling, pray for him — God gives life through the prayers of his people.
verseByVerse.note: The “sin that leads to death” is probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by those who left the church.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first of three climactic “we know” statements. The born-of-God believer does not keep on sinning — the habitual orientation of the regenerate life is away from sin, not settled into it (cf. 3:9). The protection is personal: “he who was born of God protects him” — almost certainly a reference to Christ the Son, the one who was uniquely born of God, who guards his own (Jn 10:28–29; 17:12). The evil one does not touch (haptetai) him — does not lay hold of, does not gain a controlling grip. This is not a promise of immunity from temptation or spiritual attack, but of ultimate invulnerability: the evil one cannot finally own or destroy the one Christ is keeping. The believer is not unassailed; they are undefeatable.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second “we know”: the epistle’s binary in its sharpest possible form. We are from God; the whole world lies in the evil one. The word keitai (lies) suggests passive submission — the world is not actively fighting the evil one but resting in his embrace, unaware and unresisting, like a sleeping person in the arms of an enemy. There is no neutral ground, no comfortable middle category, no third territory between the two domains. The believer lives in a world under hostile power, sustained only by the greater one within them (4:4), witnessing to a world that does not yet know it needs rescuing from the one it is resting in.

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third and culminating “we know”: the Son of God has come. The incarnation — the great fact with which the epistle opened (1:1–2) — is restated as the ground of everything. He has come, and the coming has given us understanding (dianoian) — not merely information but the cognitive and spiritual capacity to know the true God. The circle from the prologue is now complete: the eternal life that was with the Father and was made manifest (1:2) is now declared to be the true God himself. The ascription of deity to Jesus Christ — “He is the true God and eternal life” — is among the clearest in the New Testament. The one in whom we are, the one who is eternal life (v. 11), the one the Father sent — he is the true God. No qualification, no reservation.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.commentary: One of the most abrupt closings in the New Testament — and exactly right. After the theological summit of v. 20 — the true God, eternal life, the Son who has come — John ends with the most practical of warnings: guard yourselves from idols. An idol is anything that claims the place that belongs to the true God — any competing love, any false conception of God, any teacher who offers a Christ less than the one described in v. 20. In Ephesus, literal idols were everywhere; the command was not metaphorical. But the principle applies in every age and every culture: having encountered the true God, refuse every substitute. The best protection against idols is not vigilance alone but the deep, sustained, Spirit-confirmed knowledge of the one who is true. You cannot treasure the real and be satisfied with the counterfeit. Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

5.theology:
Faith as Victory. The declaration of 5:4 — "this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith" — is one of the most important statements about the nature of faith in Scripture. Faith is not a spiritual achievement, a heightened state of consciousness, or a moral virtue we cultivate. It is a hand that receives, a trust that rests, a confidence that looks away from itself to the Son of God who has already overcome. "Has overcome" — this points to the finished work of Christ at the cross as the source and ground of the believer's victory. We do not overcome the world by spiritual heroism; we overcome it by trusting the one who already has.

Assurance as Gift. The stated purpose of the letter — "that you may know that you have eternal life" (5:13) — stands as a rebuke to every theology that treats Christian assurance as presumption or spiritual pride. John writes to produce certainty. Reformed theology has always distinguished between assurance and presumption: presumption claims safety without evidence; assurance rests on the testimony of the Spirit, the evidence of new birth, and the promises of God. The three tests of the letter are not meant to produce anxiety but confirmation — the gentle hand of a faithful pastor showing the believer where the signs of life are visible. To know that you have eternal life is not arrogance; it is the appropriate response to the faithfulness of the God who cannot lie.
5.examples:
Then: The community, battered by false teaching and painful departure, needed to know one thing above all: that they had not missed it, that they were in the Son, that the life they had received was real and was eternal. John writes to give them that certainty — not a new experience, not a higher spirituality, but the settled confidence of those who have the Son and therefore have life. The simplicity of the final verdict — "whoever has the Son has life" — is both the most inclusive and most exclusive statement possible: inclusive, because anyone may have the Son; exclusive, because there is no life outside of him.

Now: In an age of therapeutic Christianity, where the goal is often feeling good about ourselves, John's letter is a corrective and a comfort. Assurance in John is not a feeling to be cultivated; it is a knowledge to be received — grounded in the testimony of God himself (5:9–10), confirmed by the evidence of new birth, and resting ultimately on the person of the Son. "This is the true God and eternal life" — Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever. Whatever else may be uncertain in a Christian life, this is not: whoever has the Son has life, and the Son cannot be taken away.
